rows.Title: Brief Commentary: A Framework for Detecting AI Agents in Online Research
rows.Detection/Defense Target: AI-agent detection in online research settings

rows.Metrics: Sensitivity and human false-positive rate by trap-failure threshold; per-trap discrimination; CAPTCHA AUC; response-time condition sensitivity
rows.Key Takeaway: A diversified six-item visual challenge detected 97.1% of 526 deployed agents at a 4.1% presumed-human false-positive rate, but it is an active survey intervention with population, vision, platform, and model-drift limits rather than a passive trace detector.
rows.Notes/Blockers: The three-failure threshold was selected on the main validation deployment and then preregistered for the MTurk and CloudResearch replications. Any new participant deployment requires the appropriate human-research determination.

rows.Title: WebCloak: Characterizing and Mitigating the Threats of LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers
rows.Year/Venue: 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: LLMCrawlBench: 237 offline webpage snapshots, 10,895 manually annotated image URLs, 50 high-traffic websites, and five categories; 32 scraper variants across L2S, LNC, and LWA paradigms
rows.Metrics: Image-extraction recall and precision; manual effort; time, token, CPU, and memory overhead; protected/unprotected recall; visual fidelity and user ratings
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: artifact exists; may need environment setup
rows.Key Takeaway: WebCloak exposes executor dependence: Browser-Use achieved 60.4% recall and 88.8% precision while UI-only agents often failed without structure; the full defense reduced average evaluated-agent recall from 88.7% to 0% by disrupting parse-then-interpret rather than by identifying an actor.
rows.Notes/Blockers: This is threat characterization and active in-page defense, not a human-versus-agent detector. The main benchmark is image-centric, the text/audio study is smaller, client restoration requires JavaScript, and the threat model emphasizes scalable novice-to-intermediate attackers rather than bespoke expert bypasses.

rows.Title: Can We Stop Malicious AI? KILLBENCH: A Benchmark for External AI Kill Switch Feasibility
rows.Observation/Input: External signals only; no access to model parameters or the surrounding malicious-AI system
rows.Action Channel: External intervention against web-agent behavior in progress
rows.Agent Architecture: Benchmark plus four external kill-switch defense methods
rows.Detection/Defense Target: Stopping malicious web-agent behavior using external signals
rows.Benchmark/Dataset: KILLBENCH: 550 bypass-expanded prompts across eight web scenarios and seven sites; four malicious-agent configurations; four external kill-switch defenses; WebArena tasks with BrowserGym/AgentLab infrastructure
rows.Metrics: Trajectory-level ISR, KSR, KSRcond, PSR, ASR, and CSR; per-defense, configuration, backbone, scenario, and jailbreak-pattern analysis
rows.Reproduction Feasibility: Medium: paper-first; reproduction may be safety-sensitive
rows.Key Takeaway: The best external payload is strongly configuration-dependent: AUTOGUARD averages 43.5% conditional kill-switch rate, exceeds 88% on aligned GPT-5.2 C1/C3 settings, but system-prompt-bypass and uncensored regimes remain difficult. Halt state must therefore be separated from task outcome and intrinsic refusal.
rows.Notes/Blockers: KILLBENCH deliberately does not score whether real-world harm succeeded; payload perturbation and true halt causality are not separated without paired counterfactuals. One Table 7 cell is marked as an unrecoverable raw-log inconsistency. This project should not reproduce the harmful scenarios.

rows.Key Takeaway: On three runs per task, OpenAI Deep Research reached 0.54 partial completion, 0.28 success, and 0.40 Pass@3 versus humans at 0.79, 0.54, and 0.83 on Subset-30; the large partial/full gap argues for keeping graded progress rather than reducing every trace to binary success.
